title: Multitasking: Switching costs
evidence: Switching between tasks can introduce time costs, especially for more complex tasks.
limitations: Institutional research overview; not a personal prediction.
application: Try keeping one task active during a work block.

title: Task Interruption in Software Development Projects
authors: Zahra Shakeri Hossein Abad and colleagues
evidence: A mixed-methods developer study found contextual factors related to interruption disruptiveness; voluntary switches were disruptive in its retrospective analysis.
limitations: Observational analysis and survey; does not establish an effect for every developer.
application: Record voluntary switches to identify situations worth changing.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: Multitasking Across Industry Projects: A Replication Study
authors: Karina Kohl, Bogdan Vasilescu, Rafael Prikladnicki
evidence: Working on fewer projects and more repetitively across days was associated with higher productivity; higher multitasking did not show an effect in this setting.
limitations: One industry setting; findings are not universal.
application: Compare your own work patterns without assuming every switch is harmful.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: The Hidden Cost of Window Management
authors: Steven Jeuris, Paolo Tell, Steven Houben, Jakob E. Bardram
evidence: The study identified time spent managing windows while switching tasks.
limitations: Studied Windows 7 interactions; modern interfaces differ.
application: Prepare the windows needed for one task before starting.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: Brief diversions vastly improve focus, researchers find
evidence: A laboratory study of a prolonged repetitive task found that brief goal diversions helped sustain performance.
limitations: University report of Ariga and Lleras research; not evidence for a specific timer schedule.
application: Experiment with a short planned break during longer work.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: Reach for your cell phone at your own risk: The cognitive costs of media choice for breaks
authors: Sanghoon Kang and Terri R. Kurtzberg
evidence: In an anagram experiment, phone-based shopping breaks were followed by poorer performance than paper or computer-based breaks.
limitations: Specific break task and participant group; not all phone use or work contexts.
application: Try a phone-free pause and reflect on returning to the task.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: Using an electronic device counteracts benefits of taking a break in nature
evidence: A study of 81 participants found improved post-break attention scores in the green-space group without laptops.
limitations: Small study with specific conditions; no guarantee for an individual.
application: If practical, try a break outdoors without optional screen use.
verificationScope: Public abstract or institutional report read; phone-break entry full text read

title: Distracted much? New research may help explain why
evidence: Experiments suggested engagement and individual differences mattered for distractibility; task difficulty alone did not explain it.
limitations: University summary of laboratory eye-tracking tasks, not a clinical assessment.
application: Choose a meaningful, concrete next task and reflect on engagement.
